headline: TeamPCP hackers arrested in Australia, linked to 1,000+ org infections
summary: Two men arrested in Australia are accused of participating in cybercrimes for TeamPCP, a prolific hacking group responsible for over 1,000 global supply chain attacks.
details: Authorities in Australia have arrested two men accused of being members of the notorious hacking group TeamPCP. This group is linked to a relentless series of supply chain attacks that compromised over 1,000 organizations worldwide in just nine months.

The arrests were announced by the Australian Federal Police, who charged the men with 14 offenses. The group's attacks primarily targeted CI/CD pipelines, lacing open-source software with malware that spread virally from package to package.

The malware, dubbed Shai-Hulud, infected future package updates and spread when developers downloaded compromised packages. A key feature was its ability to collect credentials for other packages, which TeamPCP then used to infect those as well.

One notable incident involved the infection of the Trivy vulnerability scanner, which subsequently led to the compromise of downstream packages like KICS, Telnyx Python SDK, and LiteLLM. This initial compromise resulted in the theft of terabytes of credentials and private data.

TeamPCP utilized an unconventional method for its command-and-control servers, employing Internet Computer Protocol-based canisters to ensure immunity from takedowns. This allowed the worm to rapidly change control server URLs.

Researchers suggest that the speed and scale of TeamPCP's operations may have been accelerated by the use of LLMs, significantly compressing the time and expertise traditionally required for such sophisticated cyber campaigns.
If convicted, one of the arrested men faces over 20 years in prison, while the other faces over 10 years. The FBI was also involved in the investigation.

headline_marked: [[AI Art Scraper]] Collaborates with Artist to Build Protection Tool
headline: AI Art Scraper Collaborates with Artist to Build Protection Tool
summary: After scraping 12 million images from artist platform Cara, the individual responsible is now working with the platform's founder on a new open-source tool to safeguard creators' work.
details: An artist-run platform called Cara, designed to protect artists from unauthorized AI training data scraping, was recently targeted by a massive scrape of 12 million images. The individual responsible, who posted the data online, has now surprisingly agreed to collaborate with Cara's founder, Jingna Zhang, on a new tool to help artists protect their work.

The scrape, which cost less than $10, caused significant server fees for Cara and alarmed its 1.5 million users who had sought refuge from platforms like Instagram, where content is explicitly available for AI training. This incident has highlighted the ongoing challenge of preventing data scraping, even with protective measures like Glaze, which aims to disrupt AI mimicry.

The scraper, who goes by the screen name 'Heft', initially posted the 12-terabyte archive on Reddit as a 'fun project.' However, after confronting artists and seeing the emotional toll the scrape had taken, including reports of panic attacks and deleted portfolios, Heft expressed deep regret for his actions.

Heft, a student with a background in software and digital preservation, stated that his intention was not malicious but rather a technical experiment that escalated due to trolling. He acknowledged the cruelty and thoughtlessness of his actions and the unforeseen consequences beyond causing anger.

Zhang, who founded Cara with volunteers, expressed frustration with the scraping incidents and the misconceptions surrounding the platform's ability to guarantee complete security. She noted that larger platforms are scraped more frequently, leading to greater concern for artists.

Despite the challenges, Zhang sees the collaboration with Heft as a positive development. They are working together on an open-source tool, aiming to provide a more robust solution for artists to protect their digital creations from unauthorized use in AI training.
